tone_statements.citation: Lubbe, Melissa; Priest, Tiffany; Lew, Sigrid. 2022. A preliminary phonology and Latin-based orthography of Para Naga (Jejara), Northwest Myanmar. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 15(2): i-xxiii (data paper, 26 pp.). Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press. hdl:10524/52505.
tone_statements.quote: In Para Naga, three distinct tones are present, namely, High, Mid, and Low. High and mid tones are realized with a slight drop in pitch in utterance final position. [...] Table 3 presents minimal sets for the three tones. Note that tone has a relatively low functional load; not every syllable can carry all three tones. [...] Para Naga has not only lexical but also grammatical tone. Certain lexical items can function as both nouns and verbs, with the grammatical category distinguished by tone [...]
tone_statements.locator: Section 3 'Para Naga Tone and Tone Sandhi', p. viii; see also p. i ('Para Naga is a tonal Tibeto-Burman language') and Conclusion p. xiii
tone_statements.n_tones: 3 (High 55, Mid 33, Low 11); plus grammatical tone and verb-root tone sandhi

tone_statements.citation: Barkman, Tiffany. 2015. Reduplication and Imperfectivity in Jejara (Para Naga). Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 8: 121-132. Canberra: Asia-Pacific Linguistics. hdl:1885/95250.
tone_statements.quote: It exhibits typical Tibeto-Burman characteristics such as SOV word order and contrastive tone1. [fn. 1:] Jejara is a language which makes use of contrastive tone. Yet in the orthography as Jejara speakers are currently using it, tone is not indicated. The orthographic form is the form which is used for the vernacular in Jejara examples in this paper. Without committing to a particular tonal analysis, the author attempts to indicate phonetic tone throughout the paper as much as is possible.

sources.citation: Barkman, Tiffany. 2014. A descriptive grammar of Jejara (Para Naga). MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. xxi+222 pp. (245-page PDF)
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Silent on stress. Ch. 2 'Phonology and morphology' (thesis pp. 19-28 = pp. 41-50) is a self-described 'cursory overview' whose consonant, vowel and tone charts are copied from Lubbe (2007, unpublished orthography statement). 2.2.3 Tone (p. 21): three tones (mid/high/low) with minimal pairs; 'Tone is, however, not as robust as in some languages, and there are not a great number of minimal pairs showing contrast only by tone.' 2.4 Syllable and word structure (p. 22): C1(C2)V, no codas, words 1-3 syllables, prenasalization and 'minor syllable' noted as needing further study. sources.note: States that Jejara 'makes use of contrastive tone', that the community orthography does not mark it, and that the author indicates phonetic tone in the examples 'without committing to a particular tonal analysis' (fn. 1, p. 121). No inventory or tonal analysis given.
